column3: It repeats the focus verse's claim that God expands and restricts provision, denying that abundance establishes permanent status.
It states the same expansion and restriction of provision and contrasts worldly delight with the hereafter.
The warning that God can make the earth swallow wrongdoers closely echoes Qarun's sudden swallowing.
It repeats that provision is expanded and restricted by God, directly supporting the speakers' new conclusion.
The immediately preceding verse narrates Qarun and his dwelling being swallowed, the event interpreted in 28:82.
Its unfailing reward for faith and righteous action offers only a general contrast to failed worldly prosperity.
It repeats the central formula that God expands and restricts provision as a sign for believers.
Its reference to "yesterday" within the Musa narrative is only a verbal and same-surah echo.
The prohibition on counting a gift as much is a contrastive lexical route, not support for 28:82's account of divine grace.
It explicitly presents God as the one who expands and restricts provision and replaces what is spent.
It repeats the expansion-restriction formula and grounds it in God's knowledge of servants.
The human act of calculating is contrastive with the divine measuring of provision in the focus verse.
It says most people fail to understand that expanded and restricted provision is God's measured distribution.
The same-surah phrase "if not for" divine intervention provides a limited grace-and-protection parallel.
Divine determining and guiding is a broad measure motif, without the focus verse's provision or reversal.
Guidance and misguidance here do not materially illuminate Qarun's collapse or provision.
This earlier Musa episode has no substantive link to the focus verse's interpretation of wealth and collapse.
It rejects wealth as the measure of fitness for authority and attributes God's bestowal to His choice.
Those who fear a reversal and become regretful supply a distant parallel to the onlookers' changed judgment.
The conflict in Musa's early story does not clarify the focus verse's provision or collapse themes.
It distinguishes beneficent giving from humiliating reminders, a limited contrast to receiving divine grace.
It describes God granting favor to whomever He wills among His servants, supporting the focus verse's attribution of grace.
It begins the Qarun episode, establishing the extraordinary wealth and arrogance whose end 28:82 reassesses.
God's constricting and expanding is directly relevant, though the verse applies it to lending and return.
The objection to God bestowing favor on whom He wills offers a limited parallel to contested divine allocation.
Provision is attributed to God rather than human fear or control, supporting the focus verse's causal correction.
Divine proportioning of human creation is a broad measure motif, not a provision-specific connection.
Its conclusion that disbelievers do not prosper directly echoes the focus verse's final judgment.
It shows prosperous settlements destroyed after being heedless of their livelihood, a close wealth-to-ruin parallel.
The verse's constriction language concerns Yunus's ordeal rather than provision or Qarun's collapse.
Its declaration that wrongdoers do not prosper reinforces the focus verse's closing verdict on disbelievers.
It explicitly identifies God as provider for creatures and people, countering self-grounded readings of livelihood.
The earth made expansive is only a distant lexical counterpart to the earth swallowing Qarun.
Worldly flourishing is suddenly cut down after people assume control, closely paralleling the correction of wealth-confidence.
Qarun claims his wealth came from his own knowledge, the false causal reading overturned by 28:81-82.
The word for death/time creates a contrastive lexical route but does not support the focus verse's grace reading.
It concludes that disbelievers lose when punishment becomes visible, paralleling the focus verse's denial of their success.
Pharaoh's arrogant claim of sovereignty is a same-surah backdrop but not a direct provision or collapse parallel.
It warns that God can cause the earth to swallow people, directly reinforcing the mechanism of Qarun's fate.
Its statement that sorcerers do not prosper is a close formulaic parallel to the focus verse's final clause.
Wanting death before encountering it loosely parallels desire being corrected by a later encounter.
The moon's darkening is an image of collapse, but it does not address wealth, grace, or provision.
It states that wrongdoers do not prosper, providing a close formulaic confirmation of the focus verse's conclusion.
The following verse gives the moral outcome of the Qarun narrative: no exaltation or corruption, and success for the mindful.
It warns those secure from the One above that He may make the earth swallow them, directly matching Qarun's reversal.
It affirms that wrongdoers do not prosper, echoing the focus verse's final verdict.
It contrasts apparent increase with what truly grows before God, qualifying wealth as a measure of success.
The plan to restrict others' share and its frustrated outcome parallels the instability of self-controlled wealth.
God's ownership of guidance offers a broad divine-agency parallel without the focus verse's material theme.
The claim that wealth and children prove immunity is directly opposed to Qarun's downfall and the focus verse's revaluation.
It includes people whom God caused the earth to swallow and denies that God wronged them, closely matching Qarun's fate.
Its reward for patience and goodness is a general moral-success parallel, not a close connection to provision.
Human wishing is corrected by divine ownership of the next and present life, a limited parallel to coveting Qarun's place.
The uninterrupted reward motif only broadly contrasts enduring divine recompense with fleeting worldly standing.
The poets' wandering speech does not clarify the focus verse's themes.
It directs recipients of provision to give due shares, framing wealth as entrusted distribution rather than status.
It again warns that God can make the earth swallow people, reinforcing Qarun's sudden loss of security.
It attributes rescue from punishment to divine favor, a limited parallel to the focus verse's recognition of grace.
The image of wrongdoers rushing forward at judgment supplies only a distant consequence parallel.
It combines the keys of heaven and earth with God's expansion and restriction of provision, closely matching the focus claim.
The request to take a substitute does not materially connect to provision, grace, or Qarun's collapse.
Divine power over the warned people is a broad judgment parallel without the focus verse's specific themes.
Its measured, honored night shares only the root of determining, not the provision or collapse context.
The arrogant demand for visible confirmation loosely parallels the self-exalting posture corrected in the Qarun episode.
An increase in bodily capacity is presented as a divine favor to remember, not a basis for self-exaltation.
Repentance and divine forgiveness are only a general corrective counterpart to recognizing grace after danger.
Divine determining is a broad measure motif with no direct provision or wealth connection.
Its categorical separation from disbelievers gives limited support to the focus verse's final distinction about their failure.
It directly rejects interpreting restricted provision as humiliation, the inverse error corrected by 28:82.
The mountain's collapse before divine manifestation is a distant physical-collapse parallel.
It distinguishes human boasting about favor from God's actual favor in guiding people, clarifying the focus verse's "if not for God's grace."
It calls worldly enjoyment little and the hereafter better for the mindful, supporting the focus verse's value reversal.
It explicitly speaks of provision being restricted and calibrated responsibility to what God has given.
Its reference to "yesterday" is a same-surah verbal echo, without a substantive link to the focus reading.
It connects unexpected provision with God's completion of His command and a measure set for everything.
The response to revelation and accusation of magic does not illuminate the focus verse.
It presents decrease and increase as known by exact measure, a broad analogue to measured provision.
The question about emitted fluid has no material connection to the focus verse.
Its value beyond a thousand months is only a distant contrast between true worth and visible quantity.
The accusation of fabrication does not materially connect to the focus verse.
Rescue from disgrace through a favor from God parallels the speakers' recognition that grace spared them.
God's seeing of Musa and Harun does not clarify the focus verse's themes.
It condemns recognizing God's favor and then denying it, reinforcing the need to identify grace in 28:82.
Its two expected outcomes and waiting language provide only a distant reversal-of-expectation parallel.
Exact judgment by scales is a broad measure theme, not a close provision or collapse link.
A people normalize alternating hardship and ease before sudden seizure, paralleling the misreading of changing material conditions.
The prayer for prior believers contains no material link to provision or the Qarun episode.
It distinguishes temporary worldly enjoyment from final punishment for disbelievers, qualifying apparent prosperity.
It directly says unrestricted provision would lead to transgression and that God sends it down by measure.
The parable contrasts inability with God-given good provision and generous spending, treating provision as a divine gift.
Its command for fair measure and capacity has only a broad measuring connection.
God's measuring of night and day is a broad measure motif without the focus verse's wealth or collapse theme.
The learned believers' submission to what comes from God is a distant parallel to corrected recognition of divine agency.
Inheritance shares do not materially illuminate Qarun's collapse or the interpretation of provision.
Household etiquette and privacy do not connect to the focus verse's themes.
Fasting rules and marital permissions do not materially connect to the focus verse.
Its cycles of growth, decline, and revival give only a broad change-of-condition parallel.
Its promise of success through obedience only broadly contrasts with the failure of disbelievers.
Jesus' declaration that God gave him scripture and prophethood is a general gift-from-God parallel.
The command to fear God and obey the messenger does not materially clarify the focus verse.
Qarun is told to seek the final abode with what God gave him, not to spread corruption; this is the moral frame for his downfall.
It records the crowd's wish for Qarun's position yesterday, immediately supplying the attitude reversed in 28:82.
Those given knowledge answer the admirers that God's reward is better for believers who do good and endure, directly preparing 28:82.
It forbids coveting what God has favored others with and directs people to seek God's bounty, directly correcting desire for Qarun's place.
It warns against extending one's eyes toward worldly splendor and calls God's provision better and more lasting.
It exposes the false inference that expanded provision means divine honor, the premise overturned by Qarun's collapse.
The parable of the two garden owners begins a closely related narrative examination of wealth and status.
The garden owner's abundant fruit and social power form the visible wealth-confidence that the focus verse corrects.
The wealthy owner wrongs himself by treating his flourishing garden as imperishable, a close counterpart to Qarun's false security.
He presumes lasting advantage even before God, directly exemplifying the misuse of worldly abundance.
The companion redirects the wealthy owner from self-confidence to dependence on the Creator.
It explicitly calls for acknowledging God's will and power on entering abundance, the recognition Qarun and his admirers lacked.
The threat that the garden's water may sink into the ground closely parallels the removal of a seemingly secure material base.
The owner's produce is destroyed and he regrets his investment, a close narrative parallel to the reversal after visible prosperity.
The garden owner has no supporting party besides God and cannot defend himself, matching Qarun's inability to find help.
It concludes that authority belongs to God, who is best in reward and outcome, directly expressing the focus verse's revaluation.
It explicitly subordinates wealth and children to enduring righteous deeds in reward and hope.
It lists wealth and other worldly attractions as made desirable, explaining the allure behind wishing for Qarun's position.
It redirects desire from worldly attractions to a better reward with God.
After people rejoice in opened abundance, God seizes them suddenly; this closely parallels prosperity followed by abrupt reversal.
The saved recognize that they would not have been guided without God, a close pattern of retrospective attribution to divine favor.
Hardship and ease alternate as a community is tested, supplying the context for not reading material conditions as fixed status.
It warns not to be impressed by wealth and children, which may become a means of punishment rather than honor.
It repeats that wealth and children need not signal good fortune and may accompany punishment.
Differences in provision are explicitly attributed to God's favor, denying that unequal wealth proves self-made superiority.
A town's affluent people transgress before its destruction, a broader wealth-and-ruin counterpart to the Qarun episode.
It questions whether wealth and children mean that good is being hastened to their possessors.
It answers that the possessors do not understand, directly challenging prosperity as a reliable sign of favor.
Affluent leaders regularly reject warning, providing the immediate setting for the wealth-immunity claim in the next verse.
It explicitly denies that wealth and children bring nearness to God and makes faith and righteous deeds the basis of recompense.
It treats worldly life as temporary amusement and adornment while locating reward with faith and mindfulness.
It depicts worldly wealth and boasting as vegetation that flourishes, withers, and becomes debris.
It warns that wealth and children can distract from God's remembrance, countering their use as status markers.
It calls wealth and children a trial and locates the great reward with God.
Its mention of wealth and sons occurs within a portrait of arrogant denial, a limited counterpart to prosperity without success.
It describes abundant wealth as a bestowed condition, not self-generated proof of worth.
Its mention of sons in attendance continues the portrait of privileged abundance that does not secure success.
The demand for still more after abundance illustrates the failure to recognize provision as measured grace.
It joins stinginess and self-sufficiency, directly exposing the attitude wealth can foster.
It identifies denial of the best outcome as the companion error to self-sufficiency.
It describes the resulting path toward hardship, a moral reversal of assumed ease.
It denies that wealth will avail its owner at ruin, closely qualifying material security.
It states that the human being transgresses, introducing a close diagnosis of the wealth-pride pattern.
Self-sufficiency is named as the cause of that transgression, directly relevant to Qarun's self-attribution.
It returns all people to God, completing the correction of apparent independence.
Competition for more distracts people, directly naming the acquisitive impulse behind coveting Qarun's position.
The warning that accumulation continues to the graves exposes the terminal limit of status-seeking abundance.
It condemns the collector and counter of wealth, a close ethical counterpart to wealth-centered self-regard.
It portrays someone who amasses and counts wealth as a defining moral failure.
It rejects the belief that wealth will make its owner permanent, directly paralleling the false security undone in Qarun's fate.
